_meta.name: Mini judgment corpus (England & Wales, tort and contract)
_meta.note: Short paraphrased teaching summaries of leading judgments written for this prototype. They are not the official law reports and must be checked against the reported judgment before any real use.
_meta.doctrine_tags: Each judgment is tagged with the doctrines it is authority for: 'pro' = it supports the doctrine applying / liability or enforceability being established; 'contra' = it limits or rejects it; 'mixed' = it cuts both ways.

judgments.name: Donoghue v Stevenson

passages.text: Mrs Donoghue's friend bought her a bottle of ginger beer in a cafe in Paisley. The bottle was opaque. After drinking part of it she poured out the rest and found the decomposed remains of a snail. She suffered shock and gastroenteritis. She had no contract with the manufacturer, Stevenson, because her friend had made the purchase.

The House of Lords held by a majority that the manufacturer owed the ultimate consumer a duty to take reasonable care. A manufacturer who sells products in a form showing an intention that they reach the consumer as they left him, with no reasonable possibility of intermediate examination, owes the consumer a duty of care in their preparation, and the absence of a contract is no bar to a claim in negligence.

Lord Atkin's neighbour principle: you must take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions which you can reasonably foresee would be likely to injure your neighbour, meaning persons so closely and directly affected by your act that you ought reasonably to have them in contemplation. The case is the foundation of the modern law of negligence and of manufacturers' liability to consumers.

judgments.name: Caparo Industries plc v Dickman

passages.text: Caparo bought shares in Fidelity plc and then made a takeover bid, relying on audited accounts which showed a profit. In fact the company had made a loss. Caparo sued the auditors, alleging they had been negligent in certifying the accounts and that it had lost money as an investor.

The auditors owed no duty of care to Caparo as an investor. A statutory audit is prepared for the shareholders as a body to exercise control over the company, not to guide individual decisions to buy shares, so there was insufficient proximity between the auditors and a member of the public or existing shareholder making an investment decision.

In a novel situation a duty of care requires foreseeability of damage, a relationship of proximity, and that it be fair, just and reasonable to impose a duty. The law should develop new categories of negligence incrementally and by analogy with established categories, and liability for financial loss caused by statements is limited to cases where the maker knew the statement would be relied on for a particular purpose.

judgments.name: Hedley Byrne & Co Ltd v Heller & Partners Ltd

passages.text: Advertising agents Hedley Byrne asked their bank to obtain a credit reference about a client, Easipower, from Easipower's bankers, Heller. Heller replied that Easipower was good for its ordinary business engagements, expressly 'without responsibility'. Relying on this, Hedley Byrne placed advertising orders and lost about 17,000 pounds when Easipower went into liquidation.

The House of Lords held that a duty of care in making statements can arise where there is a special relationship in which the maker assumes responsibility and knows that the recipient will reasonably rely on the statement, and that pure economic loss caused by such a negligent misstatement is recoverable. On the facts, the express disclaimer of responsibility prevented any duty arising, so the claim failed.
Liability for negligent misstatement rests on a voluntary assumption of responsibility and reasonable reliance. A clear disclaimer accompanying advice can negate the assumption of responsibility.

judgments.name: Bolam v Friern Hospital Management Committee

passages.text: Mr Bolam received electro-convulsive therapy at a mental hospital without relaxant drugs or physical restraint and without being warned of the small risk of fracture. He suffered fractures and sued, alleging negligence in the treatment and in the failure to warn him.

McNair J directed the jury that a doctor is not negligent if he acts in accordance with a practice accepted as proper by a responsible body of medical men skilled in that particular art, even if other doctors would take a different view. There were responsible bodies of opinion supporting the practice followed, and the jury found for the hospital.

The Bolam test measures a professional against the standard of a responsible body of practitioners in the same field. For decades it was also applied to the disclosure of treatment risks, until the Supreme Court departed from that approach for advice on risks in Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board.

judgments.name: Bolitho v City and Hackney Health Authority

passages.text: A two-year-old boy with breathing difficulties was in hospital. A doctor who was called failed to attend. The child suffered a cardiac arrest and catastrophic brain damage and later died. The doctor said that even if she had attended she would not have intubated him, and expert evidence was divided on whether that would have been proper.

The claim failed: a responsible body of medical opinion would not have intubated, so the failure to attend did not cause the harm. The House of Lords added that the court is not bound to accept a body of professional opinion merely because experts support it; the opinion must be capable of withstanding logical analysis and have weighed the comparative risks and benefits.

Bolitho qualifies Bolam: in rare cases a court may reject professional practice that is not reasonable or responsible. Where a breach consists of an omission, causation asks what would have happened had the duty been performed, including whether the hypothetical conduct would itself have been negligent.

judgments.name: Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board

passages.text: Mrs Montgomery, a diabetic woman of small stature, was pregnant. Her obstetrician did not tell her of the 9 to 10 per cent risk of shoulder dystocia in a vaginal delivery, or offer the alternative of a caesarean section, because she considered the risk of a grave outcome very small. Shoulder dystocia occurred and the baby was born with severe disabilities.

The Supreme Court found for Mrs Montgomery. A doctor is under a duty to take reasonable care to ensure that the patient is aware of any material risks involved in a recommended treatment and of any reasonable alternative or variant treatments. Had she been told of the risk she would probably have chosen a caesarean section and the injury would have been avoided.

A risk is material if a reasonable person in the patient's position would be likely to attach significance to it, or if the doctor is or should reasonably be aware that this particular patient would attach significance to it. The Bolam test no longer governs the disclosure of risks; the therapeutic exception is narrow and cannot be used to avoid informing patients of choices they are entitled to make.

judgments.name: Chester v Afshar

passages.text: Miss Chester underwent lumbar spine surgery performed by Mr Afshar, a neurosurgeon. He did not warn her of a 1 to 2 per cent risk of cauda equina syndrome, which materialised without negligence in the operation itself. She said that if warned she would not have had the operation that week but would have sought further advice, and might later have had the same operation with the same risk.

By a majority of three to two the House of Lords held the surgeon liable. Although conventional but-for causation was not satisfied, because the risk would have been the same on a later date, the injury was within the scope of the very risk the surgeon had a duty to warn about.

On policy grounds, causation may be established by a narrow modification of traditional principles in order to vindicate the patient's right of autonomy and to give effect to the duty to warn of material risks before consent to surgery.

judgments.name: Barnett v Chelsea and Kensington Hospital Management Committee

passages.text: Three night watchmen drank tea and began vomiting. They went to the hospital's casualty department, where the duty doctor, speaking through a nurse, told them to go home and call their own doctors. Mr Barnett later died of arsenic poisoning.

The hospital owed a duty of care to those presenting at casualty and breached it by failing to examine Mr Barnett. But the claim failed on causation because the evidence showed that he would have died even if he had been properly examined and treated, since the antidote could not have been given in time.

The but-for test: the claimant must prove on the balance of probabilities that, but for the defendant's breach, the damage would not have occurred. A breach which makes no difference to the outcome does not ground liability.

judgments.name: Overseas Tankship (UK) Ltd v Morts Dock and Engineering Co Ltd (The Wagon Mound No 1)

passages.text: The defendants' ship negligently discharged furnace oil into Sydney Harbour. The oil spread to the claimants' wharf, where welding was being carried out. Molten metal fell on cotton waste floating in the oil, the oil ignited and the wharf was badly damaged by fire.

The defendants were not liable for the fire damage because, on the evidence, it was not reasonably foreseeable that the oil would ignite on water. The Privy Council refused to follow Re Polemis, which had imposed liability for all direct consequences of negligence.
A defendant is liable only for damage of a kind or type that was reasonably foreseeable at the time of the breach. It is not enough that the damage was a direct consequence of the negligent act.

judgments.name: Smith v Leech Brain & Co Ltd

passages.text: Through his employer's negligence a worker was splashed on the lip by molten metal and burned. The burn triggered a pre-malignant condition he already had; he developed cancer and died. His widow sued the employer.

The employer was liable for the death. The burn itself was a foreseeable kind of injury, and the defendant had to take the victim as he found him, including his pre-existing susceptibility. The Wagon Mound had not abolished the thin skull rule.

The eggshell skull rule: once the type of harm is foreseeable, the tortfeasor is liable for its full extent even if that extent is greater than could have been foreseen because of the claimant's pre-existing physical vulnerability or condition.

judgments.name: Nettleship v Weston

passages.text: Mrs Weston was a learner driver. Mr Nettleship, a friend, agreed to give her lessons after checking that her insurance covered him as a passenger. On her third lesson she failed to straighten the steering wheel after a turn, mounted the pavement and hit a lamp post, injuring his knee.
The Court of Appeal held the learner liable. Her inexperience did not lower the standard of care: she was judged by the objective standard of the reasonably competent and experienced driver.

The standard of care in negligence is objective and impersonal. It does not vary with the defendant's own skill, experience or personal limitations; a defendant who undertakes an activity is held to the standard of a reasonably competent person doing it.

judgments.name: Bolton v Stone

passages.text: Miss Stone was standing on a residential road outside a cricket ground when she was hit by a ball struck out of the ground. The ground was protected by a fence, and balls had been hit out only about six times in thirty years.

The club was not negligent. Although it was foreseeable that a ball might be hit out of the ground, the probability of injury was so small that a reasonable person would not have taken further precautions against it.

Foreseeability of harm is not enough for breach. The court weighs the likelihood of harm, and a reasonable person may disregard a risk that is very small, taking into account the probability of the event and the practicability of precautions.

judgments.name: Paris v Stepney Borough Council

passages.text: Mr Paris, a garage hand, had sight in only one eye, which his employer knew. He was not given safety goggles. While he was removing a bolt, a chip of metal flew into his good eye and he became totally blind.

The employer was negligent in failing to provide goggles to this employee. Because the consequences of an eye injury were so much more serious for a one-eyed worker, the duty owed to him required that precaution even if it might not have been required for other workers.

In deciding what precautions are reasonable the court considers the gravity of the harm that may result to the particular claimant, not only the likelihood of the accident. A known vulnerability of the claimant raises the precautions required.

judgments.name: Latimer v AEC Ltd

passages.text: After an exceptionally heavy rainstorm the factory floor flooded and became slippery with an oily mixture. The employer spread all the sawdust it had, but some areas remained uncovered, and a worker slipped and was injured.

The employer was not negligent. It had taken reasonable precautions in response to the risk, and the only way to remove the risk completely would have been to close the factory, which was out of proportion to the risk.
The cost and practicability of precautions are weighed against the size of the risk. A defendant is not required to take measures that are wholly disproportionate to the danger.

judgments.name: Alcock v Chief Constable of South Yorkshire Police

passages.text: At the Hillsborough football stadium in 1989 police negligence led to a fatal crush in which many spectators died. Relatives of victims claimed for psychiatric illness. Some were elsewhere in the stadium, some watched live television coverage, and one identified a body at the mortuary about eight hours later.

All of the claims failed. Live television coverage, which did not show identifiable individuals, was not equivalent to seeing or hearing the event, and identifying a body some eight hours later was not part of the immediate aftermath.

A secondary victim must show a close tie of love and affection with the primary victim, proximity in time and space to the accident or its immediate aftermath, and perception of the event or its immediate aftermath with their own unaided senses, together with a psychiatric illness induced by sudden shock. Being told of the event by a third party is not enough.

judgments.name: McLoughlin v O'Brian

passages.text: Mrs McLoughlin's husband and three children were injured in a road accident caused by the defendant's negligence. She was told at home about two hours later and went to the hospital, where she saw her family before they had been cleaned up and learned that her youngest daughter had died. She suffered psychiatric illness.

The House of Lords allowed her claim. Although she was not at the scene, she came upon the immediate aftermath of the accident at the hospital, seeing her family in the condition caused by it, and her psychiatric injury was reasonably foreseeable.

A close relative who does not witness the accident may recover if they come upon its immediate aftermath and perceive it directly. Recovery depends on the closeness of the relationship, proximity in time and space, and the means by which the shock was caused.

judgments.name: Page v Smith

passages.text: Mr Page was involved in a moderate car collision caused by the defendant's negligence. He was physically unhurt, but the accident caused a recurrence of chronic fatigue syndrome from which he had previously suffered, and he was unable to work again.

The House of Lords held that he could recover. He was a primary victim because he was within the range of foreseeable physical injury, so it did not matter that physical injury did not in fact occur or that psychiatric injury was not itself foreseeable.

A primary victim who is directly involved and within the zone of foreseeable physical danger need not satisfy the control mechanisms applied to secondary victims, and the defendant takes the victim as found, including a pre-existing psychological vulnerability.

judgments.name: Rylands v Fletcher

passages.text: The defendant mill owners had a reservoir built on their land by independent contractors, who failed to block disused mine shafts beneath it. When the reservoir was filled, water burst through the shafts and flooded the claimant's neighbouring mine.

The defendants were liable even though they had not been negligent themselves. A person who for his own purposes brings onto his land and keeps there anything likely to do mischief if it escapes must keep it at his peril and is answerable for the damage caused by its escape.
Strict liability attaches to the escape of a dangerous thing brought onto land in the course of a non-natural use of that land, causing damage to a neighbour's property.

judgments.name: Robinson v Chief Constable of West Yorkshire Police

passages.text: Police officers tried to arrest a suspected drug dealer on a busy shopping street. In the struggle the suspect and officers fell onto Mrs Robinson, an elderly pedestrian, who was injured.

The Supreme Court held that the police owed her a duty of care. The ordinary principles of negligence apply to the police when their positive acts create a reasonably foreseeable risk of physical injury, and on the facts the officers were in breach.

Caparo did not lay down a universal three-stage test to be applied in every case. Where a case falls within an established category, such as physical injury caused by a positive act, the existing principles apply; the Caparo factors guide only the incremental development of the law in genuinely novel situations.

judgments.name: Tomlinson v Congleton Borough Council

passages.text: An eighteen-year-old dived into the shallow water of a lake in a country park run by the council, despite notices saying 'Dangerous water. No swimming'. He struck his head on the bottom and was left tetraplegic.

The council was not liable. The risk did not arise from the state of the premises but from the claimant's own choice to engage in an activity with an obvious danger, and there was no duty to protect an adult against such obvious risks.

An occupier is not generally required to protect adults from obvious risks they freely choose to run, and the social value of the activity and the cost of preventing it are relevant to what is reasonable.

judgments.name: Spartan Steel & Alloys Ltd v Martin & Co (Contractors) Ltd

passages.text: Contractors negligently cut an electricity cable supplying the claimant's steel factory. Metal in the furnace had to be removed and was damaged, and the factory lost production while the power was off.

The claimant recovered for the physical damage to the metal and the profit lost on that particular melt, which was consequential on the physical damage, but not for the profit it would have made on further melts during the power cut, which was pure economic loss.
Economic loss consequential on physical damage to the claimant's property is recoverable in negligence, but pure economic loss unconnected with such damage is generally not.

judgments.name: Wilsher v Essex Area Health Authority

passages.text: A premature baby was negligently given excess oxygen in hospital. He developed retrolental fibroplasia, causing near blindness. Excess oxygen was one of five possible causes of the condition, the others being associated with premature birth.
The claim failed because the claimant had not proved on the balance of probabilities that the excess oxygen, rather than one of the other possible causes, caused the condition.
Showing that a breach added one more possible cause to several existing ones, or materially increased the risk among distinct agents, does not discharge the burden of proving causation.

judgments.name: Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co

passages.text: The company advertised that it would pay 100 pounds to anyone who caught influenza after using its smoke ball three times a day for two weeks as directed, adding that 1,000 pounds had been deposited with the Alliance Bank to show its sincerity. Mrs Carlill used the ball as directed, caught influenza and claimed the reward.

The Court of Appeal held that the advertisement was an offer to the world of a unilateral contract, which Mrs Carlill accepted by performing the stated conditions; she did not need to notify acceptance. The deposit showed an intention to be bound, so the promise was not a mere advertising puff.

An advertisement can be an offer where its terms are clear and it shows an intention to be bound by anyone who performs the conditions. Performance of the conditions is both acceptance and consideration, and the offeror may dispense with notice of acceptance.

judgments.name: Partridge v Crittenden

passages.text: Mr Partridge placed an advertisement in a magazine reading 'Bramblefinch cocks, bramblefinch hens, 25s each'. He was prosecuted for unlawfully offering wild birds for sale.
His conviction was quashed. The advertisement was not an offer but an invitation to treat, so he had not offered the birds for sale.
Advertisements of goods for sale are ordinarily invitations to treat rather than offers, because the advertiser has limited stock and cannot sensibly be bound to sell to everyone who replies.

judgments.name: Pharmaceutical Society of Great Britain v Boots Cash Chemists (Southern) Ltd

passages.text: Boots operated a self-service shop in which customers took medicines from open shelves and paid at a cash desk supervised by a registered pharmacist. Statute required certain poisons to be sold under a pharmacist's supervision, and the Society argued that the sale took place at the shelf.
The display of goods on the shelves was an invitation to treat. The customer made an offer at the cash desk, which the shop accepted there under the pharmacist's supervision, so there was no offence.
Displaying goods with prices invites customers to make offers; the seller remains free to accept or refuse each offer.

judgments.name: Hyde v Wrench

passages.text: Wrench offered to sell his farm to Hyde for 1,000 pounds. Hyde replied offering 950 pounds, which Wrench refused. Hyde then wrote saying he would pay 1,000 pounds after all, but Wrench would not sell.
There was no contract. Hyde's counter-offer of 950 pounds rejected the original offer, which could not afterwards be revived by a purported acceptance.
A counter-offer operates as a rejection of the original offer and brings it to an end.

judgments.name: Adams v Lindsell

passages.text: The defendants wrote offering to sell wool and asked for a reply by post. Their letter was misdirected and arrived late. The claimants posted an acceptance the same evening, but before it arrived the defendants, having heard nothing, sold the wool to someone else.
A contract was formed when the letter of acceptance was posted, so the defendants were in breach by selling to another buyer.
The postal rule: where acceptance by post is reasonable, acceptance is complete as soon as the letter is posted, even if it is delayed or lost.

judgments.name: Entores Ltd v Miles Far East Corporation

passages.text: A London company made an offer by telex to agents in Amsterdam, who accepted by telex received in London. The question was whether the contract was made in England, so that the claimants could serve proceedings.
The contract was made in London, where the acceptance was received. For instantaneous communication, acceptance takes effect only when it is received by the offeror.
The postal rule does not apply to instantaneous forms of communication; acceptance must be actually communicated to the offeror.

judgments.name: Balfour v Balfour
judgments.area: Contract - intention to create legal relations

passages.text: A husband working in Ceylon promised to pay his wife 30 pounds a month while she remained in England for health reasons. The marriage later broke down and she sued for the payments.
There was no enforceable contract. Arrangements between spouses living together are generally not intended to create legal relations.
In domestic and social agreements there is a presumption that the parties do not intend to be legally bound.

judgments.name: Merritt v Merritt
judgments.area: Contract - intention to create legal relations

passages.text: After a husband left his wife he agreed to pay her 40 pounds a month and signed a note promising to transfer the jointly owned house to her if she paid off the mortgage. She did so, but he refused to transfer the house.
The agreement was enforceable because, unlike in Balfour v Balfour, the spouses were separated or about to separate when it was made.
When spouses are not living in amity the presumption against intention to create legal relations does not apply, and written terms point towards an intention to be bound.

judgments.name: Stilk v Myrick

passages.text: During a voyage two seamen deserted. The captain promised the remaining crew a share of the deserters' wages if they sailed the ship home short-handed. They did so, but the extra money was not paid.
The promise of extra pay was unenforceable for want of consideration because the crew were already bound by their existing contracts to do all they could to bring the ship home safely.
Performance of an existing contractual duty owed to the promisor is not good consideration for a promise of additional payment.

judgments.name: Williams v Roffey Bros & Nicholls (Contractors) Ltd

passages.text: Roffey, the main contractors refurbishing a block of flats, subcontracted the carpentry to Williams for 20,000 pounds. Williams got into financial difficulty because the price was too low. Roffey, which faced a penalty clause in the main contract if the work was late, promised to pay him an extra 575 pounds per completed flat. He completed more flats but was paid little of the extra money.

The promise of extra payment was enforceable. Roffey obtained a practical benefit from the promise, including avoiding the penalty and the trouble and expense of finding replacement carpenters, and there was no economic duress or fraud.

Where A promises B additional payment for performing an existing contractual obligation, and A obtains a practical benefit or obviates a disbenefit, that benefit can be good consideration provided the promise was not extracted by economic duress or fraud. Stilk v Myrick is refined rather than overruled.

judgments.name: Central London Property Trust Ltd v High Trees House Ltd

passages.text: In 1937 a block of flats was let at a ground rent of 2,500 pounds a year. Because of the war many flats were empty, and in 1940 the landlord agreed in writing to reduce the rent by half. By 1945 the flats were full again and the landlord's receiver claimed the full rent for the latter part of 1945.

Denning J held that the full rent was payable from mid-1945 because the conditions for which the reduction was made had ended. He said that the landlord would have been prevented from claiming the full rent for the war years, because the promise was intended to be acted on and was acted on.

Promissory estoppel: a promise intended to be binding, intended to be acted on and in fact acted on is binding so far as its terms properly apply, even without consideration, and it may be suspensory once the circumstances change.

judgments.name: Hadley v Baxendale

passages.text: The crankshaft of the claimants' mill broke. They engaged the defendant carriers to take it to engineers to be used as a pattern for a new one. Delivery was delayed, so the mill was idle for longer and the claimants lost profits. The carriers had not been told that the mill could not operate without the shaft.
The lost profits were not recoverable. In the ordinary course of things a mill might have a spare shaft, and the special circumstances were not communicated to the carriers.

Damages for breach of contract are recoverable for loss arising naturally, according to the usual course of things, from the breach, or for loss that may reasonably be supposed to have been in the contemplation of both parties at the time they made the contract as the probable result of its breach.

judgments.name: Victoria Laundry (Windsor) Ltd v Newman Industries Ltd

passages.text: A laundry bought a large boiler to expand its business. The sellers, an engineering company, damaged it while dismantling it and delivered it five months late. The laundry claimed the profits it would have made from the expansion and from especially lucrative dyeing contracts with the Ministry of Supply.

The laundry recovered the ordinary profits it would have made, because the sellers knew it needed the boiler for immediate use in its business. It could not recover the exceptional profits from the dyeing contracts, of which the sellers knew nothing.

Recoverable loss is that which was reasonably foreseeable as liable to result from the breach, judged by the knowledge the defendant possessed at the time of contracting, whether imputed knowledge of the ordinary course of things or actual knowledge of special circumstances.

judgments.name: Taylor v Caldwell

passages.text: Caldwell agreed to let the Surrey Gardens and Music Hall to Taylor for four days of concerts. Before the first concert the hall was destroyed by fire without the fault of either party.
Both parties were discharged. The contract was subject to an implied condition that performance would be excused if it became impossible through the perishing of the thing on which it depended.
Where performance depends on the continued existence of a specific thing, the destruction of that thing without fault discharges the contract.

judgments.name: Krell v Henry

passages.text: Henry agreed to hire Krell's flat in Pall Mall for the days of King Edward VII's coronation processions, for which the flat had been advertised as a viewing place, although the written contract did not mention the processions. He paid a deposit. The processions were cancelled because of the King's illness and Henry refused to pay the balance.

The contract was frustrated. Viewing the processions was the foundation of the contract recognised by both parties, and its cancellation defeated that common purpose, so Henry was released from paying the balance.

A contract may be frustrated not only by physical impossibility but where a supervening event destroys a state of affairs which both parties regarded as the basis of the contract, even if literal performance remains possible.

judgments.name: Herne Bay Steam Boat Co v Hutton

passages.text: Hutton chartered a steamboat to take paying passengers to see the naval review at Spithead and to cruise round the fleet. The review was cancelled, but the fleet remained at anchor, and Hutton did not use the boat.

The contract was not frustrated. Seeing the review was Hutton's own purpose and commercial venture rather than the foundation of the contract for both parties, and a cruise round the fleet was still possible.
Frustration does not apply where the event defeats only one party's purpose or makes the bargain less profitable; the risk of the venture falling short lies on the party who undertook it.

judgments.name: Davis Contractors Ltd v Fareham Urban District Council

passages.text: Contractors agreed to build 78 houses for a fixed price within eight months. Because of shortages of skilled labour and materials the work took twenty-two months and cost much more. The contractors argued the contract was frustrated so they could claim more on a quantum meruit.
The contract was not frustrated. The delay and extra cost made performance more onerous but did not make it radically different from what had been undertaken.

Frustration occurs only where, without default of either party, a contractual obligation has become incapable of being performed because the circumstances would render it a thing radically different from that which was undertaken. Hardship, inconvenience or material loss is not enough.

judgments.name: L'Estrange v F Graucob Ltd
judgments.area: Contract - incorporation of terms by signature

passages.text: Miss L'Estrange bought an automatic vending machine for her cafe and signed an order form containing, in small print, a clause excluding all express and implied warranties. The machine did not work properly.
She was bound by the exclusion clause because she had signed the document, whether or not she had read it.
A party who signs a contractual document is bound by its terms in the absence of fraud or misrepresentation, regardless of whether they read them.

judgments.name: Parker v South Eastern Railway Co
judgments.area: Contract - incorporation of terms by notice

passages.text: Mr Parker left a bag in the railway's cloakroom and received a ticket with 'see back' on the front. The back stated that the company would not be liable for any package worth more than 10 pounds. The bag was lost and Parker claimed its full value.

The Court of Appeal ordered a new trial, holding that the question was whether the railway had done what was reasonably sufficient to give notice of the conditions, not whether Parker had actually read them.
Unsigned terms on a ticket or notice are incorporated if the party relying on them took reasonable steps to bring them to the other party's attention before or at the time the contract was made.

judgments.name: Olley v Marlborough Court Ltd
judgments.area: Contract - incorporation of terms by notice

passages.text: Mr and Mrs Olley booked into a hotel at the reception desk. A notice in their bedroom said the proprietors would not be responsible for articles lost or stolen unless handed to the manageress for safe custody. Through the hotel's negligence with the room key, a thief stole Mrs Olley's furs from the room.
The hotel could not rely on the notice. The contract had been concluded at the reception desk before the guests saw the notice in the bedroom, so the exclusion clause was not part of the contract.
Terms must be brought to a party's notice before or at the time the contract is made; a notice first seen after the contract has been concluded is not incorporated.

judgments.name: Thornton v Shoe Lane Parking Ltd
judgments.area: Contract - incorporation of terms by notice

passages.text: Mr Thornton drove into an automatic multi-storey car park. A machine issued a ticket that said it was issued subject to conditions displayed on the premises. One condition, displayed inside the car park, excluded liability for personal injury. He was injured partly through the car park's negligence.

The exclusion was not incorporated. The contract was concluded when he drove up to the machine and the ticket was issued, so conditions displayed inside came too late; and a condition so onerous needed especially clear notice.

Terms referred to on a ticket issued after the contract is concluded are not incorporated, and the more onerous or unusual a clause is, the more clearly it must be brought to the other party's attention.

judgments.name: Photo Production Ltd v Securicor Transport Ltd

passages.text: Securicor contracted to provide night patrols at Photo Production's factory for a modest charge. Its patrolman deliberately lit a fire, which spread and destroyed the factory. The contract excluded Securicor's liability for injurious acts of its employees unless the act could have been foreseen and avoided by due diligence on Securicor's part.

Securicor was not liable. There is no rule of law that a fundamental breach automatically destroys an exclusion clause; whether the clause covers the breach is a question of construction, and on its clear words this clause did.

In commercial contracts between parties of equal bargaining power who allocate risks, including by insurance, a clearly worded exclusion or limitation clause will be given effect according to its true construction.

judgments.name: Interfoto Picture Library Ltd v Stiletto Visual Programmes Ltd

passages.text: A photo library sent 47 transparencies to an advertising agency with a delivery note whose conditions imposed a holding fee of 5 pounds per transparency per day after fourteen days. The agency returned them late and was billed over 3,700 pounds.
The holding fee clause was not incorporated because it was onerous and unusual and the library had not fairly and reasonably brought it to the agency's attention. A reasonable charge was substituted.
A party relying on a particularly onerous or unusual condition must show that it was fairly and reasonably brought to the other party's attention.

judgments.name: Hochster v De La Tour

passages.text: De La Tour engaged Hochster as a courier for a European tour starting on 1 June. In May he wrote saying he no longer required Hochster's services. Hochster sued before 1 June.

Hochster could sue immediately. A clear renunciation of the contract before the date for performance is an anticipatory breach entitling the innocent party to treat the contract as ended and claim damages at once.
An anticipatory repudiation allows the innocent party to accept it, terminate and sue immediately, without waiting for the date of performance.

judgments.name: Hongkong Fir Shipping Co Ltd v Kawasaki Kisen Kaisha Ltd

passages.text: A ship was chartered for twenty-four months. Because her engine-room staff were inadequate and incompetent she was unseaworthy and out of service for about twenty weeks. The charterers purported to terminate the charter.
The charterers were not entitled to terminate. The seaworthiness obligation was an innominate term, and the breach had not deprived them of substantially the whole benefit of the contract.

For breach of an innominate term, the right to terminate depends on whether the consequences of the breach are so serious as to deprive the innocent party of substantially the whole benefit it was intended to obtain.

judgments.name: Dunlop Pneumatic Tyre Co Ltd v New Garage and Motor Co Ltd

passages.text: Dunlop supplied tyres under an agreement that the dealer would not sell below list price and would pay 5 pounds for every tyre sold in breach, as liquidated damages. The dealer sold below the list price.
The sum was a genuine pre-estimate of loss and enforceable as liquidated damages rather than a penalty.

Lord Dunedin's guidelines: a sum is a penalty if it is extravagant and unconscionable compared with the greatest loss that could conceivably follow from the breach; a genuine pre-estimate of loss is enforceable.

judgments.name: Cavendish Square Holding BV v Makdessi

passages.text: Mr Makdessi sold a controlling stake in a marketing group to Cavendish. If he breached restrictive covenants, he would lose further instalments of the price and could be required to sell his remaining shares at a price excluding goodwill. He breached the covenants. The appeal was heard with ParkingEye v Beavis, about an 85 pound overstay charge.
Neither the share-sale provisions nor the parking charge were unenforceable penalties. The provisions protected legitimate interests of the innocent party.

The test for a penalty is whether the provision is a secondary obligation imposing a detriment on the contract-breaker out of all proportion to any legitimate interest of the innocent party in the enforcement of the primary obligation.

judgments.name: Fisher v Bell

passages.text: A shopkeeper displayed a flick knife in his shop window with a price ticket. He was charged with offering it for sale contrary to the Restriction of Offensive Weapons Act 1959.
He was not guilty. Giving the words their ordinary contractual meaning, displaying goods in a shop window with a price is an invitation to treat, not an offer for sale.
Goods displayed in a shop window with a price attached are an invitation to treat; the customer makes the offer.
